MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations

Lorenz K. Muller    Philippe Bich    Chiara Boretti    Hyun-Min Chang    Jiawei Zhuang    Lukas Cavigelli
Abstract

Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer’s activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3%2.3\% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11× less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

Introduction

Perhaps the central idea in recent neural network quantization strategies is the change of basis. To compute the matrix product between an input and a weight matrix, we may transform the input by a matrix PP and apply the corresponding inverse transform to the weights, leaving the product unchanged. If PP is chosen wisely, the transformed inputs and weights can be substantially easier to quantize.

Two types of transform are widely used to ease quantization. First, activations and weights may be rotated into a different basis using an orthogonal matrix MrotM_{\mathrm{rot}}. The Hadamard transform is especially popular because it can be applied in O⁡(N​log⁡N)O(N\log N) operations and tends to produce approximately Gaussian-distributed outputs (4). Second, individual channels may be rescaled using a diagonal matrix MdiagM_{\mathrm{diag}} (29, 18, 21), thereby suppressing outlying channels and balancing the quantization difficulty of activations and weights.

One potential downside of such a change of basis is that, although the weight-side transform can be absorbed into the weights at quantization time, the corresponding input transform ostensibly needs to be applied online. Prior work often avoids this cost by propagating the input transform through the network and absorbing it into preceding layers. This approach is widely used because it can eliminate the explicit runtime transform (1). However, it also introduces dependencies between layers: applying the transform to one linear layer may require modifying its normalization parameters, preceding projections, residual branches, or other connected operators.

In this paper, we argue for tolerating the overhead introduced by online transforms because keeping them online provides a different benefit: simplicity through layer locality. MACaQ confines every transform and quantization decision to a single linear layer. No neighboring layer is modified to compensate for its quantization, and no basis transform needs to be propagated through the network. Eliminating these inter-layer dependencies allows each linear layer to be calibrated, transformed, and quantized independently. This simplifies application to new architectures, enables layers to be loaded and quantized one at a time, and leads to substantially faster quantization. Furthermore, all linear layers can benefit from online basis transforms, where in some architectures not all layers can have absorbed basis transforms.

The cost of this design choice is small. MACaQ uses only a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online. Their cost grows with the input dimension, whereas the cost of the subsequent matrix multiplication also grows with the output dimension. Consequently, their relative overhead diminishes for larger layers. We measure an end-to-end decode overhead of 2.3%2.3\% for Qwen3-32B in vLLM, while obtaining a better quality-quantization-time trade-off than prior MXFP4 methods.

The main contributions of this paper are:

  • •

    We propose MACaQ, a strictly per-linear-layer pipeline for W4A4 MXFP4 quantization. MACaQ achieves higher output quality than state-of-the-art MXFP4 methods while requiring up to 11×11\times less quantization time, see Fig. 2.

  • •

    We show that retaining lightweight basis transforms online incurs only a small inference overhead while eliminating cross-layer dependencies. This simplifies engineering, see Fig. 1, enables layer-at-a-time quantization with low memory requirements, and allows the same method to work on widely different model architectures.

  • •

    We introduce Flip-Refinement, a fast Hessian-aware coordinate-descent method that improves an initial round-to-nearest quantization assignment by moving individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values.

  • •

    We provide efficient Triton kernels for MACaQ-quantized MXFP4 models in vLLM, achieving up to 3×3\times end-to-end speedup over FP16 while limiting the overhead of online transforms to 2.3%2.3\% on Qwen3-32B.

Method

Problem Formulation

We consider weight and activation quantization to MXFP4, with the matrix multiplications themselves executed in MXFP4. An MXFP4 tensor is divided into blocks of B=32B=32 elements. Each block shares an E8M0 scale, represented by eight exponent bits and no mantissa bits, while each element has an individual four-bit FP4 E2M1 code consisting of a sign bit, two exponent bits, and one mantissa bit (25).

Consider a linear layer with weight matrix W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and a calibration set of layer inputs X∈ℝN×nX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n}. Similar to GPTQ (9), we seek to minimize the layer’s output reconstruction error:

minW^⁡‖X​W⊤−X​W^⊤‖F2=∑i=1mri​H​ri⊤,\min_{\widehat{W}}\ \left\lVert XW^{\top}-X\widehat{W}^{\top}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}r_{i}Hr_{i}^{\top}, (1)

where

H=X⊤​X,ri=wi−w^i.H=X^{\top}X,\qquad r_{i}=w_{i}-\widehat{w}_{i}. (2)

Here, wiw_{i} is the ii-th row of WW, w^i\widehat{w}_{i} is its quantized reconstruction, and the input Hessian HH is shared across all output rows.

MACaQ applies a per-channel scale followed by a block-Hadamard rotation. Let D=Diag⁡(t)D=\operatorname{Diag}(t) contain the per-channel scales and let BB denote a block-diagonal Hadamard transform with blocks of size 3232. We transform the activations and weights as

X′=X​D​B,W′=W​D−1​B.X^{\prime}=XDB,\qquad W^{\prime}=WD^{-1}B. (3)

Because BB is orthogonal, the transformation preserves the unquantized linear operation:

X′​W′⊤=X​D​B​(W​D−1​B)⊤=X​W⊤.X^{\prime}{W^{\prime}}^{\top}=XDB\left(WD^{-1}B\right)^{\top}=XW^{\top}. (4)

The corresponding Hessian in the transformed basis is

H′=X′⊤​X′=B⊤​D​H​D​B.H^{\prime}={X^{\prime}}^{\top}X^{\prime}=B^{\top}DHDB. (5)

For the exponent selection and Flip-Refinement steps below, we use a ridge-regularized version

Hf=H′+λ​mean⁡(diag⁡(H′))​I.H_{f}=H^{\prime}+\lambda\,\operatorname{mean}\!\left(\operatorname{diag}(H^{\prime})\right)I. (6)

We use λ=1.0\lambda=1.0 by default.

At inference time, a MACaQ linear layer computes

y=[(x⊙t)​B]MXFP4​[W^′⁣⊤]MXFP4,y=\left[(x\odot t)B\right]_{\mathrm{MXFP4}}\left[\widehat{W}^{\prime\top}\right]_{\mathrm{MXFP4}}, (7)

where W^′\widehat{W}^{\prime} denotes the MXFP4 reconstruction of W′W^{\prime} and [⋅]MXFP4[\cdot]_{\mathrm{MXFP4}} denotes quantization to MXFP4. Thus, all activation-side transformations remain local to the linear layer.

MACaQ quantizes each layer in four steps: (i) per-channel balancing, (ii) block-Hadamard rotation, (iii) Hessian-weighted block exponent selection, and (iv) Flip-Refinement of the FP4 codes.

Online Scaling

The first transform is a per-channel scale tt. It divides the weight columns before quantization and multiplies the corresponding activation channels:

x​W⊤=(x⊙t)​(W⊘t)⊤.xW^{\top}=(x\odot t)(W\oslash t)^{\top}. (8)

The two operations cancel in the unquantized matrix multiplication, but change the distributions presented to the weight and activation quantizers.

The aim of this transformation is to reduce the magnitude of outlying activation channels while simultaneously balancing the weight columns. There is a natural trade-off: scaling down a given activation channel scales up the corresponding weight column, and vice versa (29). We choose

tj=(σjW)α(rmsjx)1−α,rmsjx=Hj​jN,t_{j}=\frac{(\sigma_{j}^{W})^{\alpha}}{(\operatorname{rms}_{j}^{x})^{1-\alpha}},\qquad\operatorname{rms}_{j}^{x}=\sqrt{\frac{H_{jj}}{N}}, (9)

where σjW\sigma_{j}^{W} is the standard deviation of weight column jj and rmsjx\operatorname{rms}_{j}^{x} is the RMS magnitude of activation channel jj, obtained directly from the diagonal of HH. We use α=0.75\alpha=0.75, chosen on a validation set (a subset of wikitext-2 train).

Channels with large activation RMS receive smaller values of tjt_{j} and are therefore attenuated before activation quantization. Conversely, weight columns with large standard deviation receive larger values of tjt_{j} and are reduced by the division W⊘tW\oslash t. The parameter α\alpha controls the trade-off between activation and weight balancing. We clamp the resulting scales to a finite range for numerical stability.

Online Micro-Rotation

After scaling, we apply a block-Hadamard rotation along the input-channel dimension. For the block-diagonal orthogonal matrix BB,

x​W⊤=(x​B)​(W​B)⊤.xW^{\top}=(xB)(WB)^{\top}. (10)

As in prior work (4), the Hadamard transform suppresses outliers by distributing concentrated channel energy across approximately Gaussian-distributed transformed channels.

We restrict the transform to blocks of size 3232, matching the MXFP4 microscaling block size. This avoids spreading an outlying channel across multiple independently scaled MXFP4 blocks (17). The same fixed transform is applied to the scaled activations online and absorbed into the transformed weights offline.

Combining scaling and rotation gives

x′=(x⊙t)​B,W′=(W⊘t)​B.x^{\prime}=(x\odot t)B,\qquad W^{\prime}=(W\oslash t)B. (11)

MACaQ first applies the per-channel scale and then the block-Hadamard transform, because the importance weighting of channels must happen in the unrotated domain.

Hessian-Weighted Exponent Selection

In MXFP4, every block shares a power-of-two E8M0 scale. Selecting this scale presents a trade-off between resolution and clipping: a smaller scale gives finer resolution around zero but may clip large values, whereas a larger scale avoids clipping at the cost of coarser quantization.

Before refining the individual FP4 codes, MACaQ screens a small set of candidate exponents independently for every weight row and MXFP4 block. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} denote one block of transformed weight row ii. For each candidate exponent ee, we round the block to the corresponding E2M1 grid and compute

Ei,ℬ​(e)=∑j∈ℬ(Hf)j​j​(Wi​j′−W^i​j′​(e))2.E_{i,\mathcal{B}}(e)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{B}}(H_{f})_{jj}\left(W^{\prime}_{ij}-\widehat{W}^{\prime}_{ij}(e)\right)^{2}. (12)

We select the exponent that minimizes Ei,ℬ​(e)E_{i,\mathcal{B}}(e).

We evaluate offsets {+1,0,−1}\{+1,0,-1\} around the standard exponent derived from the block maximum. The selected block exponent is then held fixed during Flip-Refinement.

Flip-Refinement

The exponent screen produces an initial round-to-nearest assignment of the FP4 codes. Starting from this assignment, Flip-Refinement minimizes the ridge-regularized Hessian objective by moving individual codes to adjacent E2M1 levels.

For output row ii, let

ri=wi′−w^i′,gi=Hf​ri⊤.r_{i}=w^{\prime}_{i}-\widehat{w}^{\prime}_{i},\qquad g_{i}=H_{f}r_{i}^{\top}. (13)

Suppose changing code (i,j)(i,j) changes its reconstructed value by Δ\Delta, such that

W^i​j′←W^i​j′+Δ.\widehat{W}^{\prime}_{ij}\leftarrow\widehat{W}^{\prime}_{ij}+\Delta. (14)

The residual then changes from rir_{i} to ri−Δ​ejr_{i}-\Delta e_{j}. The resulting decrease in the row objective is

gain⁡(i,j,Δ)=2​Δ​gi,j−Δ2​(Hf)j​j.\operatorname{gain}(i,j,\Delta)=2\Delta g_{i,j}-\Delta^{2}(H_{f})_{jj}. (15)

A positive gain implies an improving move. After accepting the flip, the gradient is updated incrementally:

gi←gi−Δ(Hf):,j.g_{i}\leftarrow g_{i}-\Delta(H_{f})_{:,j}. (16)

This update avoids recomputing the complete matrix-vector product after each flip.

The E2M1 grid is non-uniform, so Δ\Delta depends on the current code, the chosen direction, and the fixed block scale. At every iteration, we evaluate the adjacent levels of every code and select the single highest-gain move for each output row. The output rows are independent and are processed in parallel. Rows for which no positive-gain move remains are removed from the active set and require no further work. Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

Here, Δ∈𝒩⁡(Qi​j,si​j)\Delta\in\mathcal{N}(Q_{ij};s_{ij}) are the reconstructed-value changes associated with moving one level upward or downward on the local FP4 grid (where possible).

Each iteration accepts at most one flip per output row, so KK is also the maximum number of accepted flips per row. In practice, many rows converge before reaching this budget.

Cost of Online Transforms

The activation-side pipeline of a MACaQ linear layer is: (i) apply the per-channel scale, (ii) apply the block-Hadamard transform, and (iii) quantize the result to MXFP4. Activation quantization is required by any W4A4 MXFP4 implementation, so the additional operations introduced by MACaQ are only the scale and the micro-rotation.

For a layer processing TT tokens with input dimension nn and output dimension mm, a block-Hadamard transform of size BB requires approximately T​n​log2⁡BTn\log_{2}B additions, while the scale requires T​nTn multiplications. By comparison, the matrix multiplication performs approximately 2​T​m​n2Tmn arithmetic operations. The ratio is therefore

ConlineCmatmul=T​n​(log2⁡B+1)2​T​m​n=log2⁡B+12​m.\frac{C_{\mathrm{online}}}{C_{\mathrm{matmul}}}=\frac{Tn(\log_{2}B+1)}{2Tmn}=\frac{\log_{2}B+1}{2m}. (17)

For B=32B=32, this becomes

ConlineCmatmul=3m.\frac{C_{\mathrm{online}}}{C_{\mathrm{matmul}}}=\frac{3}{m}. (18)

Both online transforms are applied once to each input and reused across all mm output channels. Their cost is therefore independent of mm, whereas the cost of the matrix multiplication grows linearly with mm. For example, the smallest output dimension among the quantized linear layers of Llama-3-8B is m=1024m=1024, giving an arithmetic-operation ratio below 0.3%0.3\%.

This estimate describes arithmetic work rather than wall-clock performance. The measured overhead also depends on kernel fusion, memory traffic, launch overhead, and the relative throughput of FP16 and MXFP4 operations. We therefore measure the actual kernel-level and end-to-end overhead in later sections. Consistent with the analysis above, the relative overhead decreases with layer and model size.

Quantization Procedure

MACaQ preserves the layer-wise modularity of the underlying network: each linear layer has its own scaling factors, block rotation, Hessian, block exponents, and FP4 codes. Quantizing one linear layer never requires modifying a neighboring normalization layer, projection, or residual branch.

Forward hooks accumulate

Hℓ=∑kXℓ,k⊤​Xℓ,kH_{\ell}=\sum_{k}X_{\ell,k}^{\top}X_{\ell,k} (19)

for every linear layer ℓ\ell over chunks of the calibration sequence. After collecting these statistics, each linear layer is independently scaled, rotated, exponent-screened, and refined. The original layer is then replaced by its packed MXFP4 implementation.

Only the layer currently being processed needs to reside on the GPU (and for the calibration, outputs of parallel layers). The remaining model weights remain in host memory. This streaming procedure reduces peak device memory and allows the same quantization implementation to be reused across model architectures; all calibration and quantization logic is attached locally to linear layers.

Implementation Details

MACaQ offers two levers for trading quantization time against output quality: the number of calibration tokens and the maximum number KK of Flip-Refinement iterations.

We produce the Pareto curve in Fig. 2 by sweeping these two parameters. Quality begins to plateau at approximately 2×1062\times 10^{6} calibration tokens and K=512K=512 Flip-Refinement iterations. For fair comparison we use K=128K=128 and 2×1052\times 10^{5} calibration tokens for MACaQ in the experimental section (ca. 150s to quantize Llama3-8B).

Besides this, our default configuration uses block size 3232, exponent offsets {+1,0,−1}\{+1,0,-1\}, scale-balancing parameter α=0.75\alpha=0.75, and ridge coefficient λ=1.0\lambda=1.0. The parameters α\alpha and λ\lambda were chosen with a wikitext train set validation run on Llama3-8B (sensitivity plot in appendix). The Flip-Refinement implementation parallelizes across output rows and removes converged rows from the active set. We additionally compile the repeated refinement step with torch.compile; the initial compilation cost is amortized across layers with matching shapes.

Experiments

To show the effectiveness of MACaQ, we consider several different metrics. For comparison with literature baselines, we use model perplexity, as it is widely reported in quantization work and provides a continuous and comparably reliable measure of model quality.

We further report results on generative benchmarks. In generative settings, quantization errors may accumulate over generated sequences in ways that are not visible in fixed-text metrics such as perplexity, and these tasks are closer to many practical use cases. To illustrate the ease of generalization to new architectures, we also apply MACaQ to an image diffusion model. Finally, we measure the throughput of MACaQ relative to standard FP16 and other common baselines, both at the kernel level and end-to-end, and perform an ablation over the main components of MACaQ.

The models we evaluate are drawn from the Llama-3 (11), Qwen3 (30), and Qwen3.5 (23) families. We evaluate perplexity on Llama models for comparability with prior work and use the reasoning-capable Qwen models for generative reasoning evaluations. For image diffusion, we use FLUX.2 Klein 4B (3), as it is openly available.

Note that for MoE models we only quantize expert layers (also for baselines) otherwise we quantize all weights and activations, but not the embeddings and lm-head (as is customary).

All experiments are run on a recent GPU with 504 TFLOPS (FP16), 96 GB memory and 1.79 TB/s memory bandwidth and use OCP MXFP4 format.

Perplexity

For perplexity measurements, we follow related work and calibrate on the WikiText-2 training set. We evaluate on the WikiText-2 (20) and C4 (24) test sets. WikiText-2 can therefore be understood as an in-distribution evaluation with respect to the calibration data, while C4 provides an out-of-distribution evaluation. We use a context length of 20482048. The results in Tab. 1 and Fig. 2 show that MACaQ matches or outperforms the baselines also in terms of quality, not only speed.

Large-Model Quantization

MACaQ can be used to efficiently quantize models that are too large to reside on the target GPU at full precision. To demonstrate this, we quantize Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on a machine with a single 9696GB GPU. The model contains 122122B total parameters, and its FP16 weights require ca. 244244GB.

MACaQ processes the model with lazy loading of layers and reaches a GPU-memory usage of 32.532.5GB. Quantization takes 6464 minutes (with 32 flips and 512K calibration tokens) and produces a WikiText-2 perplexity of 5.145.14, compared with 5.065.06 for the full-precision model. The resulting MXFP4 model requires 7474GB of GPU memory and can run on the same 9696GB GPU. Thus, MACaQ can quantize a model that does not fit on the target GPU in its original precision into one that does.

Generative Language Tasks

Generative benchmarks are closer to many practical workloads and have the potential to reveal accumulation effects that may only appear when a model generates a sequence of tokens. They also avoid the limitations of multiple-choice QA evaluation highlighted by Dutta et al. (5).

We evaluate MACaQ-quantized dense Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 MoE models on IFEval (31) and MATH-500 (13). MATH-500 contains free-form, non-multiple-choice mathematics problems that require reasoning chains to answer correctly. IFEval tests the instruction following capabilities of models in generation.

Tab. 2 shows that MACaQ performs well on these tasks.

Image Diffusion

One of the key distinguishing features of MACaQ is that it can be applied to new architectures with minimal effort because it treats each linear layer in isolation. We demonstrate this by quantizing the linear layers of FLUX.2 Klein 4B (3) to MXFP4.

This model also offers an official NVFP4 variant11 1 for a fair comparison we quantize the same layers that this official NVFP4 model quantizes with MACaQ, which provides a strong baseline. NVFP4 uses microscaling groups of 1616, rather than the 3232 used by MXFP4, and requires approximately 4.54.5 rather than 4.254.25 bits per element.

We find that MACaQ produces a more faithful quantized model with respect to the original BF16 model when prompted with GenEval2 prompts (14). In Table 3, we report pairwise metrics ranging from signal-level similarity (PSNR), through perceptual similarity (LPIPS), to semantic similarity (DINOv3). MACaQ is closer to the original BF16 model across all these metrics. For a qualitative illustration see Fig. 4.

Kernel-Level Speed

In Table 4, we compare the speed of a single linear layer across different batch sizes and matrix dimensions. We compute 𝐗𝐖⊤\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^{\top} using square weight matrices 𝐖∈ℝN×N\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}, where N∈{4096,16384}N\in\{4096,16384\}, and inputs 𝐗∈ℝB×L×N\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times N}, where the batch size B∈{1,16}B\in\{1,16\} and context length L∈{512,16384}L\in\{512,16384\}. We compare our MACaQ MXFP4 linear layer with, first, the same kernel with online scaling and rotation disabled; second, the Marlin W4A16 kernel (10); and, finally, a FP16 baseline.

The MACaQ kernel reaches a substantial speedup over FP16, while the overhead of online scaling and rotation remains low. For the smaller layer, the overhead is at most approximately 6%6\%, and for the larger layer it remains below 3%3\%. As expected from the theoretical analysis, the relative overhead decreases for larger layers.

End-to-End Speed

On Qwen3-32B at batch 1, our MACaQ MXFP4 implementation decodes at 69.8 tok/s against 22.8 for FP16 (3.06x); at batch 256 the gain is 5252.8 vs 3061.5 tok/s. Per-batch-size numbers for both models are in the appendix. MACaQ achieves up to 3×3\times end-to-end speed-up over FP16. Generally, speed-ups are comparable to Marlin (10) in the memory-bound case and outperform Marlin in compute-bound settings.

In Fig. 3, we isolate the overhead caused by online rotation and scaling. For the small Qwen3-0.6B model, this overhead is approximately 8%8\%(i.e., MACaQ still provides a substantial speedup over FP16). As explained in the Method section, the overhead decreases with model size, reaching approximately 2%2\% for Qwen3-32B.

Ablation

In Table 5, we show the contributions of the main components of MACaQ. Each component provides an improvement of a similar order of magnitude, and their combination achieves the lowest quantization error.

Related Work

Hessian-Based Weight Compression

Much of the current second-order quantization literature builds on Optimal Brain Damage (OBD) (15) and Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) (12) that introduced Hessian-based model compression. Optimal Brain Compression (OBC) (8) adapted this framework to layer-wise compression and introduced Optimal Brain Quantization (OBQ), using the layer-input Hessian H=X⊤​XH=X^{\top}X to minimize output reconstruction error. GPTQ (9) subsequently made this approach scalable to large language models by fixing the quantization order, allowing the same Hessian factorization to be reused across output rows. These methods assign weights sequentially and compensate the remaining unquantized weights. In contrast, MACaQ begins from a cheap RTN assignment and then revisits the individual codes through incremental Hessian-aware updates.

Coordinate-Descent Quantization

QuantEase (2) and CDQuant (22) also formulate quantization (pure weight-quantization) as coordinate descent and improve over one-shot assignments such as GPTQ by revisiting quantized weights. Our Flip-Refinement is designed primarily for speed in weight and activation quantization. It keeps each MXFP4 block exponent fixed and considers only the two E2M1 levels adjacent to the current code, allowing closed-form evaluation of the gain of each move.

Basis Transforms

Basis transforms have become a central tool for reducing weight and activation quantization error. QuIP (4) popularized incoherence processing through Hadamard transforms for weight quantization, and QuaRot (1) extended Hadamard rotations to weight–activation quantization. SmoothQuant (29) used element-wise scaling to balance errors between activations and weights. Later work has optimized the rotation itself (19, 16), general per-layer affine maps, as in FlatQuant (28), or an element-wise scale, including weight-only quantization with AWQ (18) and calibration-free weight quantization with SINQ (21)

For microscaling formats, block-local rotations are often preferable to full-channel rotations, e.g. MR-GPTQ (6) and (27, 17), as they avoid spreading an outlier across multiple independently scaled quantization blocks. Other work has studied how these transforms interact: (7) analyze the sources of error in weight–activation quantization and recommend combining rotation and scaling, while (26) show that reducing concentrated activation mass makes Hadamard transforms more effective preconditioners.

Limitations

The core design decision of MACaQ, keeping everything layer-local, means that cross-layer error compensation is impossible. A secondary pass with cross-layer statistics could be added on top, but would likely incur the slower quantization times of other methods.

In our MoE experiments we restricted ourselves to expert quantization only due to practicality considerations.

For the smallest model tested (0.6B parameters) the online basis transform overhead climbs to 8%8\%, which starts to be relevant for some settings.

Conclusion

We have introduced MACaQ, a fast and easy to apply MXFP4 quantization method for models based on linear layers. MACaQ matches or outperforms state of the art methods in quality and is faster. The key concepts that enable this are a light-weight Flip-Refinement to replace GPTQ, a novel Hessian-aware shared-scale optimization, and light-weight online basis transforms that enable the quantization processing to be local to each linear layer. All these features combined enable us to quantize a 122B Qwen3.5 model in 64 minutes while using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

Appendix 0.B Pareto-Plot Numerical Details

Here we report the numbers relating to the plot in Fig. 2 in Tab. 7.

Hyperparameter sensitivity

We find that MACaQ is not very sensitive to hyperparameter selection (see Fig. 5)

OCP MXFP4 compliance

The OCP MXFP4 specification requires the shared block scale to be a power of two (E8M0). The DuQuant++ codebase provides both cast_to_eBm0() and cast_to_eBm0_improved(), the latter permitting fractional-power-of-two scales, which are more expressive but not representable in the E8M0 scale field. We use a compliant cast throughout, for all methods including our own, which accounts for a small discrepancy with some of the numbers reported in the DuQuant++ paper.

Appendix 0.C Extending Flip-Refinement to Vector-Quantized Weights

Flip-Refinement can also refine vector-quantized weights by replacing a codeword rather than a scalar code. We apply this extension to the IQ3_S and IQ3_XXS weight-only formats in llama.cpp.

Codebook constraints.

Both formats encode four consecutive weight magnitudes with one codebook index: IQ3_S has 512512 codewords and IQ3_XXS has 256256. Each group of 3232 weights shares a 4-bit scale code kk, and each group of 256256 weights shares an FP16 scale dd. A reconstructed weight is w^j=d​f​(k)​σj​cj\widehat{w}_{j}=d\,f(k)\,\sigma_{j}c_{j}, where cc is a codeword and σj∈{±1}\sigma_{j}\in\{\pm 1\}. The scale factors are f⁡(k)=1+2​kf(k)=1+2k for IQ3_S and f⁡(k)=(k+0.5)/2f(k)=(k+0.5)/2 for IQ3_XXS. Signs are independent in llama.cpp’s IQ3_S format; IQ3_XXS permits only the 128128 even-parity sign patterns within each group of eight weights.

Changing one magnitude while holding the others fixed often produces a tuple outside the codebook. Scalar Flip-Refinement therefore has few legal moves, motivating a search over complete codewords.

Block refinement.

We retain the regularized row objective from Sec. Flip-Refinement, Li=ri​Hf​ri⊤L_{i}=r_{i}H_{f}r_{i}^{\top} with ri=wi′−w^i′r_{i}=w^{\prime}_{i}-\widehat{w}^{\prime}_{i} and gi=Hf​ri⊤g_{i}=H_{f}r_{i}^{\top}. Recall that for a scalar move of size Δ\Delta on input jj, Eq. (15) gives the exact decrease 2​Δ​gi,j−Δ2​(Hf)j​j2\Delta g_{i,j}-\Delta^{2}(H_{f})_{jj}. A block move is the same statement with vectors. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} contain the four input indices of one block, let vv and uu be its current and candidate reconstructions, and write A=(Hf)ℬ,ℬA=(H_{f})_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B}} and δ=u−v\delta=u-v. Then

gain⁡(i,ℬ,u)=2​δ⊤​gi,ℬ−δ⊤​A​δ.\operatorname{gain}(i,\mathcal{B},u)=2\,\delta^{\top}g_{i,\mathcal{B}}-\delta^{\top}A\,\delta. (20)

The expression is exact because the objective is quadratic: a change confined to four coordinates is described completely by the gradient on those coordinates and the 4×44\times 4 Hessian block. Interactions with the other n−4n-4 weights of the row are already contained in gi,ℬg_{i,\mathcal{B}}.

Eq. (20) has a geometric reading that makes the search natural. Completing the square gives

gain⁡(i,ℬ,u)\displaystyle\operatorname{gain}(i,\mathcal{B},u) =const−(u−ui⋆)⊤​A​(u−ui⋆),\displaystyle=\text{const}-(u-u_{i}^{\star})^{\top}A\,(u-u_{i}^{\star}), (21)
ui⋆\displaystyle u_{i}^{\star} =v+A−1​gi,ℬ.\displaystyle=v+A^{-1}g_{i,\mathcal{B}}.

Here ui⋆u_{i}^{\star} is the value the four weights would take if they were not quantized (the exact minimizer over the block with all other weights fixed, i.e. one Newton step on the block), and the best codeword is the one nearest to ui⋆u_{i}^{\star} in the metric defined by AA. Block refinement is therefore a nearest-neighbour search: for every row and block, find the admissible codeword closest to that row’s target. In the scalar case of the main text this search has two candidates, the adjacent levels, so its cost never mattered. Here it has up to 81928192 candidates, and we organize it accordingly.

We score all admissible candidates and accept the best improving move. For IQ3_S, this means jointly searching magnitudes and signs over 512×16=8192512\times 16=8192 signed codewords. For IQ3_XXS, we alternate between selecting one of 256256 codewords with signs fixed and selecting one of 128128 legal sign patterns per eight-weight group with magnitudes fixed. Each search is exact conditional on the quantities held fixed.

Efficient exact scoring.

A nearest-neighbour search under a quadratic metric is evaluated the same way as the assignment step of kk-means: expand the square. Dropping the terms of Eq. (21) that do not depend on uu leaves

Si​(u)\displaystyle S_{i}(u) =u⊤​A​u⏟codeword “length”−2​u⊤​qi⏟match to row ​i,\displaystyle=\underbrace{u^{\top}A\,u}_{\text{codeword ``length''}}-2\,\underbrace{u^{\top}q_{i}}_{\text{match to row }i}, (22)
qi\displaystyle q_{i} =A​v+gi,ℬ.\displaystyle=Av+g_{i,\mathcal{B}}.

and the codeword with the smallest SiS_{i} is the nearest one. The two terms have very different costs. The length term u⊤​A​uu^{\top}Au depends on the codeword and on the column block, but not on the row: the metric AA is a block of HfH_{f}, which is shared by all mm output rows of the layer. It is therefore a table with one entry per codeword, computed once per block and reused by every row. The match term is a dot product between the row’s 4-vector qiq_{i} and the codeword. Computing it for all rows and all candidates at once is a single matrix product, Q​𝒞⊤Q\,\mathcal{C}^{\top}, where Q∈ℝm×4Q\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times 4} stacks the qiq_{i} and 𝒞∈ℝC×4\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times 4} stacks the candidates. The score matrix (m×C)(m\times C) is the table broadcast over rows minus twice this product, and a row-wise argmin selects the codewords.

The block scale enters as a per-row scalar: a candidate is u=si​cu=s_{i}c with cc a signed codeword, so Si​(si​c)=si2​c⊤​A​c−2​si​qi⊤​cS_{i}(s_{i}c)=s_{i}^{2}\,c^{\top}Ac-2s_{i}\,q_{i}^{\top}c, and the table and the product are combined with per-row factors. The table itself is obtained with one small product per block: with vec⁡(c​c⊤)∈ℝ16\operatorname{vec}(cc^{\top})\in\mathbb{R}^{16} precomputed for every codeword, the CC lengths are vec⁡(c​c⊤)⋅vec⁡(A)\operatorname{vec}(cc^{\top})\cdot\operatorname{vec}(A), a (C×16)​(16)(C\times 16)(16) product.

For IQ3_S the 1616 sign patterns of a block are folded into the codebook, so one table of C=8192C=8192 lengths serves all rows. For IQ3_XXS the signs are held fixed during the magnitude search and differ between rows, so the metric becomes row-dependent, (σi​σi⊤)⊙A(\sigma_{i}\sigma_{i}^{\top})\odot A: the table is now computed per row, as an (m×16)​(16×256)(m\times 16)(16\times 256) product, which is still one GEMM. The sign search over the 128128 parity-legal patterns of an 8-group has the same structure with the magnitudes μi\mu_{i} fixed and the metric (μi​μi⊤)⊙(Hf)ℬ,ℬ(\mu_{i}\mu_{i}^{\top})\odot(H_{f})_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{B}} on the 8×88\times 8 block: an (m×64)​(64×128)(m\times 64)(64\times 128) product for the lengths and an (m×8)​(8×128)(m\times 8)(8\times 128) product for the matches.

After a block is replaced in a set of rows, the gradients of those rows are corrected exactly with the rank-4 analogue of Eq. (16),

gi←gi−(Hf):,ℬ(u−v),g_{i}\leftarrow g_{i}-(H_{f})_{:,\mathcal{B}}\,(u-v), (23)

which adds four Hessian columns at a cost of 4​n4n per changed row instead of the n2n^{2} of a fresh Hf​ri⊤H_{f}r_{i}^{\top}. Only rows that accepted a move are touched.

Sweeps and cost.

Rows are processed in parallel, while blocks are visited sequentially in random order using the updated gradients. We require a relative improvement above 10−610^{-6} and recompute the gradients once per sweep to limit numerical drift. Refinement stops after at most eight sweeps or when a sweep accepts no move.

Per sweep over the n/4n/4 blocks of an IQ3_S tensor, the match products amount to 2​m​n​C2mnC operations in total, the length tables to O⁡(n​C)O(nC), and the gradient updates to at most O⁡(m​n2)O(mn^{2}) (if every row moved at every block; in practice far fewer), the same order as the once-per-sweep gradient refresh. The search thus scales linearly with the codebook size and never re-evaluates a full row objective. For the down projection of Qwen3-4B (m=2560m=2560, n=9728n=9728) with C=8192C=8192, the match products are 4.1×10114.1\times 10^{11} operations per sweep. The inner dimension of these products is only four and the blocks are processed sequentially, so peak GPU throughput is not reached; eight sweeps of such a tensor, including the sign and scale stages, take approximately 55–88 s. The FP32 score matrix is the only sizeable intermediate (8484 MB at these dimensions); for larger tensors we process rows in chunks to keep it below 600600 MB. All score products use FP32 with TF32 disabled, because the score differences between neighbouring candidates can be small. Self-tests on real GGUF tensors check monotone sweeps, agreement with brute-force block minimization, and bit-exact repacking.

Optional scale refinement.

With codes and signs fixed, we can also refine the shared scales. For a group 𝒮\mathcal{S} reconstructed as a​zaz, define A𝒮=(Hf)𝒮,𝒮A_{\mathcal{S}}=(H_{f})_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}} and q=A𝒮​v+gi,𝒮q=A_{\mathcal{S}}v+g_{i,\mathcal{S}}. Up to a constant, the objective is

L⁡(a)=a2​z⊤​A𝒮​z−2​a​z⊤​q.L(a)=a^{2}z^{\top}A_{\mathcal{S}}z-2a\,z^{\top}q. (24)

We evaluate all 1616 sub-block scale codes. For the super-block scale, zz includes the sub-block factors, and we round the continuous minimizer

d⋆=z⊤​qz⊤​A𝒮​zd^{\star}=\frac{z^{\top}q}{z^{\top}A_{\mathcal{S}}z} (25)

to FP16. Scale changes are accepted only when they reduce the objective. When enabled, these two scale stages follow the code and sign searches in each sweep.

Setup.

We quantize Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-14B with llama.cpp after applying MACaQ’s scaling and block-Hadamard rotation. The corresponding activation transform runs online in a patched llama.cpp. Hessians are estimated from 10610^{6} WikiText-2 training tokens, transformed into the quantization basis, and regularized with λ=1\lambda=1. The output head uses the Hessian of the final-normalization output.

We compare the initial quantization, scalar flips restricted to legal on-grid moves with K=512K=512, and eight sweeps of block refinement. Initial files are quantized either with or without llama.cpp’s importance matrix, computed from the same calibration text. Perplexity is measured with llama-perplexity on WikiText-2 and a Pile sample; these measurements are not directly comparable to Tab. 1.

Results.

Block refinement is most effective without an importance matrix (Tab. 8). On Qwen3-4B in plain IQ3_S, it reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 13.0613.06 to 11.8111.81, compared with 12.3112.31 for scalar flips and 11.8311.83 for importance-matrix initialization alone. On Qwen3-4B, block refinement reduces individual tensors’ Hessian objectives by 3030–42%42\%, versus 1616–32%32\% for scalar flips, and takes approximately 55–88 seconds per large tensor.

With importance-matrix initialization, the gains depend on the format. Refinement changes IQ3_S perplexity only slightly, but improves IQ3_XXS on both models. Among the refinements, block search performs best at 44B, while scalar flips perform best at 1414B. Exact block minimization thus does not guarantee better model perplexity: the searches can reach different local minima, and the layer objective is only a proxy for model quality.

Scale refinement further reduces the calibration objective but does not improve perplexity over codes-only refinement in the 44B comparisons. We therefore recommend codes-only block refinement for these formats.
